name: The Casimir Effect
statement: Two neutral plates held a whisker apart in a vacuum feel a faint force pushing them together.
statementAccent: feel a faint force pushing them together
meaning: The Casimir effect is a small attractive force that arises between two very close, parallel, uncharged conducting plates in a vacuum, produced by the quantum fluctuations of the electromagnetic field. Even empty space is filled with the restless zero-point fluctuations of quantum fields, and the plates restrict which of these vacuum modes can exist in the gap between them. Because fewer modes fit inside than outside, the vacuum pressure pushing inward exceeds that pushing outward, and the plates are drawn together. Predicted by Hendrik Casimir in 1948 and measured precisely by the late 1990s, it is one of the most striking demonstrations that the quantum vacuum is not truly empty but has real, measurable physical consequences.
mechanism: Quantum field theory assigns even the vacuum a zero-point energy, with electromagnetic field modes of every wavelength fluctuating constantly. Between two closely spaced conducting plates, only modes whose wavelengths fit the gap are allowed, so the density of vacuum modes inside is lower than in the open space outside. The imbalance in the radiation pressure of these fluctuations, greater outside than in, presses the plates together. The resulting force per unit area is tiny and falls off extremely steeply, scaling as the inverse fourth power of the separation, and involves both Planck's constant and the speed of light, marking it as an intrinsically quantum and relativistic effect. It becomes appreciable only at separations of nanometres to a fraction of a micron.

examples.text: Hendrik Casimir predicted the force in 1948 while at Philips, following discussions with Niels Bohr about the zero-point energy of the vacuum.
Steve Lamoreaux measured the force precisely in 1997, and Mohideen and Roy in 1998, confirming it is a real, quantitative effect and not merely theoretical.
At nanometre separations the Casimir force can pull together the moving parts of microelectromechanical systems, causing them to stick, a practical concern in nanotechnology.

variants.name: The Casimir-Polder force
variants.text: The related retarded, long-range limit of the van der Waals interaction between neutral atoms or between an atom and a surface, arising from the same vacuum fluctuations.

variants.name: Geometry dependence
variants.text: The force is normally attractive for parallel plates, but its sign and strength can in principle be modified by different geometries and materials.

whyItMatters: The Casimir effect is one of the clearest windows onto the reality of the quantum vacuum, showing that zero-point fluctuations of quantum fields exert a measurable force on ordinary matter. It bears on foundational questions about vacuum energy and its puzzling relationship to the cosmological constant, and it has become a practical concern in nanotechnology, where at the smallest scales it can cause the delicate parts of microelectromechanical systems to stick together.

working.text: place two conducting surfaces close together so fewer field fluctuations fit between them than outside, unbalancing the vacuum pressure.
treat the attraction as scaling with the inverse fourth power of separation, negligible except at nanometre-to-submicron gaps.
account for the Casimir force in nanotechnology, where it can cause stiction between closely spaced moving components.

limits: The force is real and measured, not merely theoretical, but it is exceedingly small and appreciable only at sub-micron separations, falling as the inverse fourth power of distance, so it is irrelevant at everyday scales. It is normally attractive for parallel plates, though geometry and materials can in principle alter its sign and magnitude. It is related to, but distinct from, the ordinary van der Waals force, being its retarded long-range limit. There is even an interpretive debate, with some physicists arguing the force can be derived without invoking zero-point energy at all, so its existence is certain while its deepest interpretation is still discussed.
misreadings: The Casimir effect is a genuine, experimentally confirmed force, not a mere thought experiment, though it is far too weak to notice except at the tiniest separations. It is not the same as the classical van der Waals force between molecules, but its retarded long-range cousin. And while it is usually described in terms of vacuum zero-point energy, this is not the only valid framing; some derivations recast it as a relativistic force between the charges in the plates, so the effect is settled even where its interpretation remains open.
origin: Predicted by the Dutch physicist Hendrik Casimir in 1948, working at Philips Research, and confirmed by precision measurements from Steve Lamoreaux in 1997 and Mohideen and Roy in 1998.
